full_text:
Interviewer:	When did you start the placement?

Subject:	Erm I started in July on the fifteenth.

Interviewer:	So you’ve been here quite a while now? 

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Do you finish in July?

Subject:	July yeah as well. 

Interviewer:	Okay can you tell me a bit about the company that you work for?

Subject:	Right. Erm the company it’s er, they make erm like chemicals. But I’m like a; the [town] site is like the production line. So it’s more for manufacturing erm pesticides, herbicides, homicides and containing the plant basically.

Interviewer:	Okay how would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	Oh, er.

Interviewer:	Are there lots of women working here?

Subject:	A lot of women chemists. (Right) But er not many engineers, chemical engineers. They’re I’ve done head counts before, there are about five engineers to twenty chemists. And there will be like probably one or two women engineers in there. Um I wouldn’t say that there are any like biases towards the gender but I think it’s quite fair. 

Interviewer:	Okay. I’ll probably ask you some questions about that later on. How useful do you think that your degree course has been to the work that you’re doing so far?

Subject:	It’s very relevant in, because I’m in manufacturing support and it’s very technical. So basically it’s really applying what I’ve learnt in the University to, but I see now in plant. So it’s not bad. (Okay) It’s keeping the mind oiled.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Are there any particular skills from University that you found useful?

Subject:	Erm problem solving may be. That’s the only main one I think. 

Interviewer:	Okay is there anything that you wish you had learnt at Uni before you started the placement that would have been useful? 

Subject:	In [company]? 

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Er well not really because we cover like the basics in the first and second year and because there such a, there’s so many things you can learn so, it’s all about develop, growing on what you path and move on further in that, that kind. 

Interviewer:	Okay, do you think that at Uni they could teach you anything about, not necessarily just the technical skills, but things like dealing with other people? Or is that just something that you learn on placement?

Subject:	No actually in, in the course, in the Chemical Engineering Course, we do have a lot of team work, project works. (Yeah) And that has helped in terms of working with other people but applying to real work this, you, you can’t really have all of it, just, yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay were you taught anything about health and safety at University?

Subject:	Yeah just some, one module.

Interviewer:	Was that helpful or? 

Subject:	It makes us aware of the potential hazards, sort of here in the industry.

Interviewer:	Did you have to do health and safety training when you arrived here?

Subject:	Oh yeah. Well I’m part of scheme now. It’s called Health and Safety erm mentoring, I think. Because they’ve identified that the main causes for like accident and things like that happen to new, new starters. (Oh right) And people, so they’ve, they’ve come up with this scheme, that I’m on. Here. Two [??]. So it’s just getting somebody whose more familiar with the work around them. And you know just get to talk with them and things like that. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that’s a good idea? 

Subject:	Erm I’ve only done one session. So I’m not sure how, how useful that is. But hopefully yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay do you think that the University could have done anything else to prepare you for going on placement at all?

Subject:	How can they do what they have already done? 

Interviewer:	You are happy with everything they did before you went on placement to prepare you? 

Subject:	I think I did more or less, I can say yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Before you started the placement, did anyone at the University on in your department say what they hoped you’d get out of going on placement? Or whether they thought going on placement was a good idea? 

Subject:	Yeah the lecturers do encourage us to go on placement because they, because of the experience and how it would help you in your final year. So that’s. They did tell you that it’s really beneficial. 

Interviewer:	Okay. How have you found the transition from education to starting work? 

Subject:	Erm it’s a bit difficult at first, especially here. But because you have to, pursue, like this sort of, especially the male population problem. You go out on plant and all you can see in the control room is men and if then you want to start asking them questions, they be like, ‘What are you doing here?’ That kind of thing. 

Interviewer:	Yeah like they don’t expect to see …

Subject:	They don’t expect to see a girl on the plant so. That’s at the beginning but, as time goes on. 

Interviewer:	Once they get used to you, its okay? 

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Have you had to face any new issues at all, like dealing with the boss or office politics or anything like that?

Subject:	Erm as in personally or?

Interviewer:	Yeah. 

Subject:	Um. Not the immediate boss, but the boss’s boss. (Yeah) But she’s a bit. She’s not on the right tracks or erm. I - I don’t really deal directly with her so it’s just about coming into the office and. It’s just, I don’t know, anything. 

Interviewer:	But you get on with everyone and everything?

Subject:	Yeah just everyone but just this particular lady. It was the lady that we saw just now as we walked in here. 

Interviewer:	Okay do you think that’s how everyone feels about her? 

Subject:	Erm she’s a lesbian. So there, there a general conception that, you know. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. Okay, do you think that your educational experience reflects what it’s like industry at all? 

Subject:	Yeah. In, since, the kind of work that you do. (Yeah) And the kind of projects that be handling. Yeah pretty much.

Interviewer:	Okay, how do you feel about going back to Uni when you finished your placement? Are you looking forward to going back or do you think it will be difficult getting back into do that sort of work or?

Subject:	Not really. I’m kind of looking forward to applying the things that you’ve learnt here. Taking it back to the University to see how it helps the studies. 

Interviewer:	Okay how do you think that work and the University differ?

Subject:	Right working in University always answers. When your working at the work because you don’t have answers so. A lot of thing is your judgement, so that’s very different from. 

Interviewer:	Has that been difficult to get used to? 

Subject:	Er slightly, a little bit. At the beginning especially. (Yeah) But right now when you got a bit more of a firm footing, so I can make judgements. Hopefully better judgements than before. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	As you get more experienced?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay, do you think that University and work have different priorities and goals?

Subject:	Erm yes I would say so. Universities are about getting the right answer. Not so much of the way, is how I feel. But here it’s about the development stage. 

Interviewer:	Yeah, and more about the process?

Subject:	The process yeah. 

Interviewer:	And at University it’s more about the final outcome?

Subject:	Well a little bit of both being in the University. But here is more about the process because the final outcome is up to anybody’s guess, so. 

Interviewer:	Okay, how big is [company]? Do you know how many people they employ here? 

Subject:	On this site?

Interviewer:	Yeah. It’s an international company, isn’t it?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	I looked on the website and it looks massive. 

Subject:	Oh we don’t own all of it. (Oh okay) Here it’s, it’s, there are four companies on site. (Okay) Yeah and [company] is the biggest of the four but I don’t know how much, how many people are there. 

Interviewer:	Do you think - I was going to say how many women do they employ? You said like about your area. And you said like when you go into the, in the plant it’s mostly men ... 

Subject:	Is. I only know of one women engineer on plant. (Okay) Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay do [company] have a structural programme in place for the placement students? 

Subject:	Um. No. The would have like projects. (Yeah) But and then when, when they’ve got students they just allocate these projects to them. 

Interviewer:	And they use specific projects for placement students or could they really be given to anyone? 

Subject:	They could be given to anyone, so it’s real stuff that we’re doing. Erm they have a lot of training packages. And, in the research group and we’re encouraged to go for all that. (Okay) Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Do they say what they hope you to achieve in the year that you’re here or anything like that?

Subject:	No. 

Interviewer:	Okay. 

Subject:	It’s more about doing the work really. 

Interviewer:	Okay. And you’re happy with that? Or would you like to have some set goals you’re supposed to do? 

Subject:	Yeah I like to know like what kind of, what, how have I developed, the skills that are developed here from first day and what I’ve done, and the last day and about erm, more specific skills rather than just work. Although we don’t get that here. 

Interviewer:	Okay what does your role in the company involve? What do you do?

Subject:	Me? I’m in the technical, I’m in the technical side of manufacturing support side, so I, my role is to support the plant. Er one of the plants on site. Erm and like do, erm problem solving things, like they encounter problems on plants, poblems and things like that. And I’ve got a year long project erm that’s on-going so that is. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Have you worked on different projects or are you just working on that one project or? 

Subject:	That’s the main one and I get bits.

Interviewer:	To do at the same time?

Subject:	Yes. Yeah.

Interviewer:	Okay is it what you expected or what you were told to expect before you started?

Subject:	When I was. When I started here, I didn’t know what the job was. I was just told it’s manufacturing support. (Okay) That’s it. Then nothing else. (Okay) Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you have any like promotional information about [company] before you started? Did they send you anything? Or did you look on the website or anything like that?

Subject:	They didn’t send, send but I looked on the website but it’s not really what is going on [town] works, cos that’s like the, downstream already. It’s like more selling and what their aim is and research that’s going on. But not what’s happening in the works site itself. (Yeah) We’re up, we’re the, we’re the upstream so, so what. And like production. And the technical kind. 

Interviewer:	So, do you think it would have been useful to have more information about?

Subject:	Yes. We’ve actually talked about the fact before in the conferences. 

Interviewer:	Okay. I mean do they think that it would help you? Have they agreed with you, [company]?

Subject:	Yes, they’ve actually. They said they were going to do that for, future. Because like a chemist now, erm my colleague, if somebody asks him in the pub what does he do? What does, who does he work for? He say, I work for [company]. What do they do? Produce pesticides. Oh so do you produce, make the pesticide? But he isn’t. They do like a lot, like the research works. So it’s more, it’s better if they can tell you what the role involves. And things like that. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility? 

Subject:	Yeah I would say so, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that [company] have been supportive of you as a new recruit or a new placement student? 

Subject:	Yeah, I think so. 

Interviewer:	Have they let you get on with the projects by yourself or have they been very involved in helping or have they let you find your own feet and, but they’re approachable if you do need help or? 

Subject:	They do support erm. But I will more, quite a lot of the times I’m left to do my own work, research and gather information and things like that. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. Are you happy with how that is or? Would you like? 

Subject:	Erm no. Personally I would like more like, monitoring. 

Interviewer:	Or like guidance?

Subject:	Guidance. (Yeah) Because I can be heading anywhere, I don’t know if it’s really helpful or not. 

Interviewer:	Okay, how would you summarise your placement experience so far?

Subject:	I think it’s really good. If - if what I’ve got here and I go back to University, it would, I have feel that it would really help me doing like lab work, erm, and maybe problem solving, thinking, projects. But as in personal development, I don’t see much I can take away from here. (Okay) Yeah.

Interviewer:	Would you recommend other people to do a placement?

Subject:	Here?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	Yeah actually it’s a really, really good place where you can basically erm. For a student you thinking wise, I think yes. It would be. 

Interviewer:	Okay. What would you say have been the best and worst things about the placement so far? 

Subject:	The best thing is, completing a proper project. Er that has taken, that has been somebody suggested and there wasn’t basically wasn’t any information and all I had to go and do everything myself. And I managed to finish that project. And do a cost-benefit kind of thing. And fed back to the plant side, so that was, the highlight, I think. 

Interviewer:	So you can see your achievements?

Subject:	Yeah. Well yeah. It’s basically saying no, we’re not going to do that. But it’s something. The worst thing so far is ongoing work with the year long project. Because it’s really slow. And I’m used to erm doing things fast in the University. A month, you finish it, you get your answer. Submit and that’s it. But erm here it’s really long, really tedious and you go for weekly meetings and. 

Interviewer:	So you don’t really see much progress?

Subject:	Don’t see much progress. But my manager said he had definitely has been identified, we’ve been able to identify things that we have not before, so hopefully that will be good for. Otherwise it’s just a long tedious thing. 

Interviewer:	Okay has the placement met your expectations? Is there anything that you thought that you would achieve on placement but haven’t yet?

Subject:	Not really. I came here just to learn what. But have, having some feedback from other people in the company, I felt that there, there’s so much more that, than just work. There’s personal development and outside training and things like that. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Are there any drawbacks to doing the placement? 

Subject:	Drawbacks? 

Interviewer:	Or is everything about it good? 

Subject:	Other than spending another year in er at the University as a student, don’t think so. I don’t think you can say there’s any drawbacks. 

Interviewer:	Yeah everything’s positive that you get out of it?

Subject:	Positive yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay you were saying about personal development and that you don’t really think that you’ve developed personally? Why do you think that is?

Subject:	Erm I know you can’t compare but comparing to, and he’s my friend was in another company. They have like meeting twice a month to see how you have progressed and how you can work better in what ways. Erm a lot of them people relational skills, that, you know have been sort of a top there. (Yeah) But here it’s just erm like doing your own work and going to meetings, doing small projects. 

Interviewer:	Okay. So do you think that goes back to the idea of having like a structure in place for (Yeah) placement students?

Subject:	I don’t think there is much structure here. It’s just, when there’s training, it comes up, on site, you go. I have to ask if I could attend them er Institute of Chemical Engineers Conference but I didn’t get to go. As in it’s, I feel that’s better understanding than, you know the role of the chemical engineer better that way. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that you will use what you’re learning on placement when you go back to Uni?

Subject:	Would I use any of it?

Interviewer:	Yeah the skills that you’ve learnt.

Subject:	I don’t know. Hopefully I will. As in my thinking, analytical skills wise, yeah. 

Interviewer:	Do you have to do a final year project or anything like that when you go back to Uni? 

Subject:	A dissertation. 

Interviewer:	Do you think you will use anything you’ve learnt here for that?

Subject:	Yeah. To me it’s very relevant, because the title I was given for the dissertation, is the, is a (slurry?) reactors. And [company] everywhere has (slurry?) reactors and we have lot of data information and experience. (Okay) So I hope to get that in the dissertation. 

Interviewer:	Are there any other students on placement here?

Subject:	There are, yeah.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Subject:	They’re all male.

Interviewer:	Are they?

Subject:	Yes. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’re all treated equally?

Subject:	I feel I’m treated better. 

Interviewer:	Why do you think that is? 

Subject:	Erm I think when they allocated the job, I don’t know how I got the, the projects that I’d got, but it seems, it feels cleaner and feels erm, I don’t know. Easier for er a woman to do. 

Interviewer:	Do you think they maybe felt, we won’t give her the dirty jobs?

Subject:	It’s not exactly clean what I’m doing. I still have to go up on plant and nasty part of the plant, but I don’t have to do what my other placement friend is doing. Everyday checking valves. Just to see, see if it’s leaking. And going at the far side of the plant. (Yeah) And going to the really old plant. I got the new one. 

Interviewer:	Are you pleased about that then? Or do you feel …

Subject:	Relatively. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay, do you think it’s been an advantage or disadvantage having other students on placement with you?

Subject:	Um. I never thought about that, but I think it’s er a good thing, advantage.

Interviewer:	Do you? Are you able to share your experiences and support each other?

Subject:	Yeah. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Would you have liked to have another female placement student or doesn’t that bother you?

Subject:	Erm. Don’t mind but erm I don’t feel like there’s any difference because I look on as if we are students. (Yeah) It’s not I’m girl, you two are boys. (Yeah) Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay, do you think that you’re treated, all of the students are treated, the same as the permanent members of staff? Or are you treated like ‘the students?’

Subject:	We get made fun of. We get took fun at but more or less treated the same. 

Interviewer:	What sort of things do they say when they’re making fun?

Subject:	Er oh filing, lets make her do it. Or erm what else? Just like, there sort of like, oh jobs that we don’t want to do, give them. And that kind of thing. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that is because you’re a student? Or because you’re female as well? 

Subject:	I think it’s because more because I’m a student, not like I’m female or anything. 

Interviewer:	Does that annoy you at all or don’t you mind?

Subject:	Erm because I come from a different culture, different background, I found the sarcasm of getting to me a little bit when I just started, but after that I found that that’s the way it is, so I’ve come to accept it. (Yeah) Yeah. 

Interviewer:	So sarcasm isn’t normal in your culture?

Subject:	No. It’s like being. I couldn’t tell if, it was real or whether it was. 

Interviewer:	Like whether they meant what they said or were just joking? 

Subject:	Yeah. But they was er, just is, it was just, yeah. But I got used to it at the end so. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay, do the projects that you’re involved in, involve a lot of team and group work or are you working on your own most of the time? 

Subject:	I can’t just work on my own for that project. Because I need to get feedback from the plant. But that’s just about the only time I work with a group of people. Erm other times basically I’m on my own, but I get help from my manager, quite often. So. 

Interviewer:	Are there any particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with? 

Subject:	I like the guys on plant, cos’ they’re really nice. Because they, initially they were like, ‘What she doing here?’ Bother’. But after that they realise I’m just here to get the information. And maybe because the way I approached them is less authori - you know? (Yeah) So they’re more forthcoming with problems. 

Interviewer:	So now they’re quite helpful? 

Subject:	They are, I like, yeah. There some of my colleagues at work.

Interviewer:	How did you react when they were, like ‘oh what’s a woman doing here’? 

Subject:	Er just go ahead on and just ask, get what I wanted, get out. (Yeah) Yeah. And but after a while, I got, I could sit down there and I could get them to tell me like slowly, and if I don’t understand, I can, it’s just like normal chatting. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think at all that may be more helpful because you are a women as well?

Subject:	Probably. Yeah I think so, because my colleague in my office has said, ‘Why do they tell you so many things?’ ‘Why when we go up, they never tell us anything?’ So, and it’s just, because of the attitude of the people on the plant as well I think it’s not just solely because I’m a girl, yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay. How do you think working with other people at work compares to doing team work say at Uni? Do you think they’re similar situations? Or is it totally different? 

Subject:	Quite similar actually I would say. (Yeah) They are those who really want to get things done. But there are those that couldn’t care less. (Yeah) I think it’s the same. 

Interviewer:	So the group work that you do at Uni is quite useful for learning how to react to situations at work?

Subject:	Yes. But erm, but there is more of a sense of importance here of course. Like if, that in if you feel an urgency to do that, because of pressures from (Yeah) the plant, from your managers. Other than that, it’s about the same I think. 

Interviewer:	Okay I think you said that you’ve got a Health and Safety mentor? 

Subject:	Yes. 

Interviewer:	Or have you got another mentor at all?

Subject:	No. 

Interviewer:	Okay. 

Subject:	Just one. 

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s a good idea to have a mentor? Have you just got the health and safety mentor to talk to you about health and safety issues?

Subject:	Not really. 

Interviewer:	Or can you talk to them about other things?

Subject:	Yes. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that, that’s a good thing? Having someone you can go to? 

Subject:	Yes but I feel that if you, I feel that it’s still better to get someone you’re close with at work and you can talk to them rather than someone labelled as a mentor and, just knowing that is a mentor’s sort of like, you feel that kind of, you wouldn’t go and tell your mentor everything you want to know, but you would go and tell somebody that you close with at work, what you’re feeling about things. 

Interviewer:	So would you say that there’s people that you work with, that aren’t called a mentor, but you maybe treat more like a mentor?

Subject:	I treat.

Interviewer:	Your colleagues?

Subject:	I yeah. I would treat them as my mentor rather than the person labelled a mentor.

Interviewer:	Yeah because you’ve already got better relationship.

Subject:	Better relationship, yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay would you rather have a different mentor or are you happy with the mentor?

Subject:	Um, I’m happy with my mentor. 

Interviewer:	Okay have you ever been given any bad advice by your mentor? 

Subject:	Er no. Not unless real advice but just joking (Yeah) bad advice, yeah. 

Interviewer:	Okay, is there anyone in the company that you’d say is like a role model to you?

Subject:	Certain aspects of certain people. 

Interviewer:	Yeah that’s what someone else said. 

Subject:	Really? Yeah but. 

Interviewer:	What is it about different people that you think makes them a role model? 

Subject:	From one, work wise, the way he approaches things, I think that’s, I would say he’s a role model for that. But a role model for treating other people and giving other people respect is another aspect. And also, yeah, that’s the two main ones. 

Interviewer:	Okay has anyone from the University been to visit you on placement? Why did they tell you that they were coming to visit you? 

Subject:	Oh yeah they took, er Professor basically just wanted to know how I’m getting along at work. It wasn’t erm, er academic thing. It was just more of welfare. Just want to know how you’re getting along and if there’s any problem at least there’s a chance to tell somebody in University what’s your situation like. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. Did you know the person that came to visit you?

Subject:	It’s a lecturer. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. Would you be happy to tell that person if you did have any problems? 

Subject:	Yeah. I - I didn’t so. But I didn’t have any (Yeah) major problems here so. 

Interviewer:	Are you in contact with them? Or anyone else, any other members of staff at University while you’re here still, so that if you say had a problem now, you could email them or?

Subject:	We were told we can email our in er personal tutor but I’ve not done it, kept in contact with him. (Okay) Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Did they visit your manager as well? 

Subject:	The visiting Professor did. But not my [?]. The person that. We get industrial tutors, they call it. (Yeah) So we’re all assigned one and he did came, visit to me and my manager. (Yeah) We sat down and had, had a chat and. 

Interviewer:	Altogether? 

Subject:	Together and also individually. 

Interviewer:	Right. Okay do you know if the University or work have a complaints procedure if you did have any problems at all? 

Subject:	I’m not aware of that, but I was aware that I can always get hold of my industrial tutor if anything happens at work that I’m not satisfied with or if. Up to now I’m fine. 

Interviewer:	Good. Do you think that there are appropriate facilities for women here?

Subject:	Yes actually. Yes.

Interviewer:	So most people that are working in companies like this are, I think this more relates to people that are working on building sites. There might not be women’s toilets ...

Subject:	But I was surprised there are women’s toilets on plant when there’s no women on plant. Yes, so. 

Interviewer:	Do you have to wear protective clothing or anything like that when you go on plant?

Subject:	Yeah definitely. 

Interviewer:	And does that fit you and?

Subject:	No, they never do. 

Interviewer:	Is that they are always for men?

Subject:	Yes. There, I got extra small but they still don’t fit me and all I got was, all they come in one size. Eat more chocolates. So, that’s. 

Interviewer:	Do things like that annoy you or?

Subject:	Oh no. 

Interviewer:	Okay. 

Subject:	Because all the women wear the same kind of clothes in there, so. 

Interviewer:	It’s only a …

Subject:	Oversized together. Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Can you think of any occasions when you think that your gender and the fact that you’re a woman has determined reactions from your colleagues or the outcome to particular events? If that makes sense?

Subject:	Not really

Interviewer:	Has anything ever happened, like similar to like when you said when you first went into the plant? (Yeah) That you felt like they were like ‘Oh what’s a women doing here?’ Has anything else like that happened or have you ever done anything when you think that the reaction that you’ve got is because you’re a female?

Subject:	No. Can’t think of any.

Interviewer:	That’s good. I’m nearly finished now. Do you want a career in engineering, chemical engineering?

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Still? 

Subject:	Still want but not in - because we can do so many things. (Yeah) I think I just came to conclusion, and I don’t want to be in manufacturing support. I prefer. Because I feel my personality, I like to go out and you know, more. Get involved in more things rather than sitting down and problem solving. 

Interviewer:	Yeah. So you still think that your placement has been useful, even if it’s to say no, this isn’t what I want to do?

Subject:	Yes. It’s useful in a sense that I know that it’s going help me in my work back in the University. But it has also helped me determine what I want to do when I get out. So, see. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that even if you want to do something different when you finish University, do you think that the placement will still help you get a job?

Subject:	Yes. Definitely. 

Interviewer:	Okay. Do you think that you know what sort of area you do want to go into? 

Subject:	I know I don’t want to be in manufacturing support. Erm it helped me eliminate the possibility of being a consultant, because that’s what consultants do. I would like to. Sorry what’s the question again? 

Interviewer:	What sort of field in chemical engineering do you think that you would want to go into?

Subject:	Right. Field as in what sort of industry?

Interviewer:	Yeah like you said you don’t want to do manufacturing support.

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Which areas would, do you think you would like to go into?

Subject:	Um. I don’t mind research. I’d probably, bit of a. I don’t know really. 

Interviewer:	That’s okay.

Subject:	Yeah. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that you would rather have a managerial role or would you like to be doing technical things still?

Subject:	I like to be specialised in technical things. 

Interviewer:	Yeah?

Subject:	And a bit of managerial but I don’t want to be wholly managerial. 

Interviewer:	Okay do you think that your placement experience will help you cope when you start work after graduation? 

Subject:	Yes. Especially the starting bit.

Interviewer:	Yeah do you think it won’t be so scary when (No) you start work for real?

turns.text: What sort of things do they say when they’re making fun?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er oh filing, lets make her do it. Or erm what else? Just like, there sort of like, oh jobs that we don’t want to do, give them. And that kind of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that is because you’re a student? Or because you’re female as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s because more because I’m a student, not like I’m female or anything.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that annoy you at all or don’t you mind?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm because I come from a different culture, different background, I found the sarcasm of getting to me a little bit when I just started, but after that I found that that’s the way it is, so I’ve come to accept it. (Yeah) Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So sarcasm isn’t normal in your culture?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. It’s like being. I couldn’t tell if, it was real or whether it was.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Like whether they meant what they said or were just joking?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. But they was er, just is, it was just, yeah. But I got used to it at the end so. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, do the projects that you’re involved in, involve a lot of team and group work or are you working on your own most of the time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I can’t just work on my own for that project. Because I need to get feedback from the plant. But that’s just about the only time I work with a group of people. Erm other times basically I’m on my own, but I get help from my manager, quite often. So.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are there any particular people that you’ve liked or disliked working with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I like the guys on plant, cos’ they’re really nice. Because they, initially they were like, ‘What she doing here?’ Bother’. But after that they realise I’m just here to get the information. And maybe because the way I approached them is less authori - you know? (Yeah) So they’re more forthcoming with problems.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So now they’re quite helpful?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They are, I like, yeah. There some of my colleagues at work.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How did you react when they were, like ‘oh what’s a woman doing here’?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er just go ahead on and just ask, get what I wanted, get out. (Yeah) Yeah. And but after a while, I got, I could sit down there and I could get them to tell me like slowly, and if I don’t understand, I can, it’s just like normal chatting.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think at all that may be more helpful because you are a women as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Probably. Yeah I think so, because my colleague in my office has said, ‘Why do they tell you so many things?’ ‘Why when we go up, they never tell us anything?’ So, and it’s just, because of the attitude of the people on the plant as well I think it’s not just solely because I’m a girl, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. How do you think working with other people at work compares to doing team work say at Uni? Do you think they’re similar situations? Or is it totally different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Quite similar actually I would say. (Yeah) They are those who really want to get things done. But there are those that couldn’t care less. (Yeah) I think it’s the same.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So the group work that you do at Uni is quite useful for learning how to react to situations at work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. But erm, but there is more of a sense of importance here of course. Like if, that in if you feel an urgency to do that, because of pressures from (Yeah) the plant, from your managers. Other than that, it’s about the same I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay I think you said that you’ve got a Health and Safety mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Or have you got another mentor at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Just one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s a good idea to have a mentor? Have you just got the health and safety mentor to talk to you about health and safety issues?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Or can you talk to them about other things?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think that, that’s a good thing? Having someone you can go to?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes but I feel that if you, I feel that it’s still better to get someone you’re close with at work and you can talk to them rather than someone labelled as a mentor and, just knowing that is a mentor’s sort of like, you feel that kind of, you wouldn’t go and tell your mentor everything you want to know, but you would go and tell somebody that you close with at work, what you’re feeling about things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So would you say that there’s people that you work with, that aren’t called a mentor, but you maybe treat more like a mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I treat.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Your colleagues?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I yeah. I would treat them as my mentor rather than the person labelled a mentor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah because you’ve already got better relationship.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Better relationship, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay would you rather have a different mentor or are you happy with the mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I’m happy with my mentor.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay have you ever been given any bad advice by your mentor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er no. Not unless real advice but just joking (Yeah) bad advice, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay, is there anyone in the company that you’d say is like a role model to you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Certain aspects of certain people.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah that’s what someone else said.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Really? Yeah but.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What is it about different people that you think makes them a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: From one, work wise, the way he approaches things, I think that’s, I would say he’s a role model for that. But a role model for treating other people and giving other people respect is another aspect. And also, yeah, that’s the two main ones.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay has anyone from the University been to visit you on placement? Why did they tell you that they were coming to visit you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh yeah they took, er Professor basically just wanted to know how I’m getting along at work. It wasn’t erm, er academic thing. It was just more of welfare. Just want to know how you’re getting along and if there’s any problem at least there’s a chance to tell somebody in University what’s your situation like.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Did you know the person that came to visit you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s a lecturer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Would you be happy to tell that person if you did have any problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I - I didn’t so. But I didn’t have any (Yeah) major problems here so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you in contact with them? Or anyone else, any other members of staff at University while you’re here still, so that if you say had a problem now, you could email them or?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: We were told we can email our in er personal tutor but I’ve not done it, kept in contact with him. (Okay) Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did they visit your manager as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The visiting Professor did. But not my [?]. The person that. We get industrial tutors, they call it. (Yeah) So we’re all assigned one and he did came, visit to me and my manager. (Yeah) We sat down and had, had a chat and.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Altogether?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Together and also individually.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right. Okay do you know if the University or work have a complaints procedure if you did have any problems at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m not aware of that, but I was aware that I can always get hold of my industrial tutor if anything happens at work that I’m not satisfied with or if. Up to now I’m fine.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Good. Do you think that there are appropriate facilities for women here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes actually. Yes.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So most people that are working in companies like this are, I think this more relates to people that are working on building sites. There might not be women’s toilets ...

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: But I was surprised there are women’s toilets on plant when there’s no women on plant. Yes, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you have to wear protective clothing or anything like that when you go on plant?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And does that fit you and?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, they never do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that they are always for men?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. There, I got extra small but they still don’t fit me and all I got was, all they come in one size. Eat more chocolates. So, that’s.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do things like that annoy you or?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because all the women wear the same kind of clothes in there, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It’s only a …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oversized together. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Can you think of any occasions when you think that your gender and the fact that you’re a woman has determined reactions from your colleagues or the outcome to particular events? If that makes sense?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not really

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has anything ever happened, like similar to like when you said when you first went into the plant? (Yeah) That you felt like they were like ‘Oh what’s a women doing here?’ Has anything else like that happened or have you ever done anything when you think that the reaction that you’ve got is because you’re a female?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No. Can’t think of any.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s good. I’m nearly finished now. Do you want a career in engineering, chemical engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Still?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Still want but not in - because we can do so many things. (Yeah) I think I just came to conclusion, and I don’t want to be in manufacturing support. I prefer. Because I feel my personality, I like to go out and you know, more. Get involved in more things rather than sitting down and problem solving.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. So you still think that your placement has been useful, even if it’s to say no, this isn’t what I want to do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. It’s useful in a sense that I know that it’s going help me in my work back in the University. But it has also helped me determine what I want to do when I get out. So, see.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that even if you want to do something different when you finish University, do you think that the placement will still help you get a job?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Definitely.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Do you think that you know what sort of area you do want to go into?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I know I don’t want to be in manufacturing support. Erm it helped me eliminate the possibility of being a consultant, because that’s what consultants do. I would like to. Sorry what’s the question again?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of field in chemical engineering do you think that you would want to go into?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Right. Field as in what sort of industry?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah like you said you don’t want to do manufacturing support.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Which areas would, do you think you would like to go into?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um. I don’t mind research. I’d probably, bit of a. I don’t know really.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s okay.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you would rather have a managerial role or would you like to be doing technical things still?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I like to be specialised in technical things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: And a bit of managerial but I don’t want to be wholly managerial.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay do you think that your placement experience will help you cope when you start work after graduation?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes. Especially the starting bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah do you think it won’t be so scary when (No) you start work for real?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I think so. It’s given me a lot of confidence when facing, dealing with things that you’re not certain about. That’s it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you work for [company] when you finish?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: [Company] in [country], I wouldn’t mind. [Company] here, no.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that because they just do manufacturing?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They just do manufacturing support.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Okay how, how have you found like moving to [town]?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has that been okay or has that been scary or? Did you know anyone here at all before you started?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No I didn’t. I stayed at the Halls of Residents for a week and that was terrible. But I was lucky because the person who lives under me, is from France and he was doing his placement here as well. (Oh right) So I knew somebody the first day I came here. I was working at the same place. And after that I found a house, student house and I moved there. And I go to church and I make some friends and after that I everything has been so good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you’re quite settled now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I wouldn’t want to leave now.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think having moved to somewhere totally different, that experience will help you when you finish University as well? When you finish Uni, do you think there’s a particular place that you’d like to go to work or would you be happy to go anywhere where there was a good job or?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I would be happy to go to anywhere where there’s a good job. But yeah I wouldn’t like, where I want to stay and find the kinds the of jobs that I’ll be getting. If I was to work with [company] in [town], and it’s a dead place. I don’t mind if the job is challenging and.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. If it’s the right job?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If it’s the right job, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay these are some questions that I asked you last time just to see whether since working your opinion has changed. What five words would you use to describe your experience in engineering so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Experience of engineering. Oh excuse me. Er specialised. Um not oh, it’s not one word, but its not as dirty as I thought it would be. Er interesting. Some bits are challenging. Can be boring sometimes as well.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay. Would you still describe it as male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes it will always be male dominated, that’s what I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Always. Why do you think that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm probably not for ever. But probably for a long time to come, is going to be male. You it, it’s a man’s world, if you’re in engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that is because like you just said you thought it would be more dirty?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I thought it would be.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s why more girls don’t do it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. And also well, I can say for myself as well, girls like to be the in the nice office. You don’t have to wear like oversized shoes and oversized coat, when you go to plant. Probably that might be a factor. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay what advantages and disadvantages do you think there are to being a woman in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Advantages, you can get jobs done easier, I think. Er but dis - disadvantage to be probably just at the beginning when people don’t know what you’re capable of. They see you as a pain and probably a bother.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Because they think that they’ll have to help you?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: They will have to help me yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that you have to work harder to show people that you don’t need their help or? Or that you’re as good as a male student or male worker?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I didn’t feel the need to work harder. No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay that’s fine. Does it bother you at all that there are so few women in engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Not now. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is that because you’ve got used to working with men more?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You think that you’re bothered it? You were a bit concerned about it before?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I was concerned yes. Because I came here to look at the place before I started work and I was concerned that I was the only girl in the office. But after that, they didn’t, didn’t bother me. Probably it’s just getting used to the same people around you.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Okay do you still think that women should be encouraged into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um yeah, I wouldn’t stop women coming to do engineering. But I still feel that yet there are actually really some aspects of men that can get job done in the chemic - in - in the engineering industry. There are certain women, they will be like, forceful and authoritative and things, but always I feel that they are more men’s qualities. (Yeah) So I would.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So generally you think that men have the characteristics you need to in engineering more (Some, yeah. Yeah) than women. (Yeah) So that’s probably with the reason why not so many women do it.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. That’s like the general picture.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Okay that’s everything. Thank you very much.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, you’re welcome.
